Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

text.text: Broad traits predict consequential life outcomes but are ill-suited to causal inference, whereas single narrow, behaviorally measured traits are more interpretable causally but predict weakly.
The space of narrow traits is also so large that choosing among them is challenging.
I propose the Power of Narrow Traits (PNT) framework to address both challenges.

In a specific person, the causal effect of a narrow trait (e.g., talkativeness) on a specific outcome (e.g., social capital) accumulates across the situations in which the trait can be expressed as a state (e.g., talking) and in which that state influences the outcome, with situations described by their features.

In its basic form, four factors multiply at each point of the feature space: (a) how often per year the person encounters such situations, (b) over how many years, (c) how strongly the trait translates into the state there, and (d) how strongly that state causally affects the outcome.
These contributions are then summed over the situations the person encounters.

The decomposition clarifies when narrow traits should be consequential, which traits to measure for a given outcome, why the same trait level leads to an outcome for some people but not for others, and how interventions can be tailored to each person's trait and situational profile.
I formalize the framework, illustrate it with worked examples, relate it to existing theories, and derive six empirical predictions.
PNT thus provides a unifying structure for future work on stable individual differences and life outcomes.

Personality traits and cognitive abilities are among the most robust correlates of consequential life outcomes.

For example, personality traits are associated with subjective wellbeing (Anglim et al., 2020; Soto, 2019), mental and physical health (Jokela et al., 2013; McGeehan et al., 2026), educational attainment (Duckworth et al., 2019; Poropat, 2009), income (Denissen et al., 2018), and interpersonal outcomes such as divorce (Roberts et al., 2007) and social status (Grosz, van Aert, & Back, 2024).

text.text: However, research on the consequences of individual differences confronts two profound methodological challenges that limit its ability to move from association to causal inference.
The first challenge concerns a trade-off between predictive validity and causal interpretability.

Although broad measures of personality and intelligence predict life outcomes reasonably well, they are composite variables rather than unidimensional traits (e.g., Grosz, 2026; Revelle, 2024; van der Maas et al., 2014).

text.text: Narrower and behavioral measures are nevertheless better suited to causal inference in two respects.
They satisfy the consistency assumption, and they are more amenable to manipulation than trait levels because they are closer to the concrete behavior.

The dilemma is that the broad measures with the strongest predictive power are the least suitable for causal inference and intervention, whereas the narrow, behaviorally anchored measures of single narrow traits that are better suited have weaker associations with outcomes.
The second challenge concerns the proliferation of narrow traits.

Because life circumstances vary widely and interact with genetic, biological, and developmental differences to produce innumerable specific behavioral tendencies, there are essentially countless narrow traits one could assess (e.g., Condon et al., 2020; Mõttus et al., 2017; Revelle et al., 2011).

text.text: However, such screening cannot tell a researcher which of the surviving traits are likely to have a substantial causal effect on a given outcome.
The prospect of an unguided choice among thousands of candidates deters some researchers from studying narrow traits at all.
Researchers who nevertheless study narrow traits often select them by intuition or convention.
This practice risks under-sampling of the tendencies that matter most for the outcome at hand.
To address both challenges, I propose the Power of Narrow Traits (PNT) framework.

Its central claim is that, in a specific person, the causal effect of a narrow trait (e.g., talkativeness) on a specific outcome (e.g., well-being, longevity, or income) accumulates across the situations in which the trait can be expressed as a state and in which that state influences the outcome.
The state can be a behavior (e.g., talking), but also an affect (e.g., anxiety), a cognition (e.g., ruminating), or a desire (e.g., desire for social status).

In the framework's basic form, four factors are multiplied at each configuration of situation features: (a) how often per year the person encounters situations with those features, (b) over how many years the trait is expressed in them, (c) how strongly the trait translates into the state there (trait expressivity), and (d) the average causal effect of the expressed state on the outcome there.
These contributions are then summed over all the situations the person encounters.

Extensions of this basic form cover diminishing returns, outcomes that return to a set point, interactions among behaviors and among narrow traits, and trait-driven situation selection (see Extensions).

The contribution of the PNT framework is to formalize a multiplicative decomposition that (a) reconciles the predictive-causal dilemma, (b) provides an operational criterion for choosing which narrow traits to measure for a given outcome and population, (c) yields tractable chains of causal effects that differ from the predictions of broad-trait and interactionist accounts, and (d) motivates tailored, situation-aware interventions.

The PNT framework is deliberately a coarse-grained model in the sense of Smaldino (2020): it reproduces qualitative patterns (orderings, contrasts, and the conditions under which trait-outcome effects appear or vanish) rather than exact effect sizes.

text.text: The values in the examples that follow are therefore order-ofmagnitude calibrations rather than parameter estimates.

That said, the framework's main purpose is to serve as a template from which fine-grained, empirically calibrated models (instances) can be built for a specific narrow trait, outcome, and population by estimating their components.
Consider two employees, Nora and Ben, who are equally good at quantitative reasoning: both score one standard deviation above the mean.
Nora is a portfolio analyst.
In a typical year she makes about 1,700 decisions that involve quantities, with about $6,000 at stake in the average decision.
Ben is a communications manager.
He makes about as many quantitative decisions, 1,500 a year, but with about $700 at stake in the average one.
In every such decision, better quantitative reasoning improves the result a little.
Suppose that one standard deviation of the ability is worth 0.1% of the amount at stake, through sounder valuations, avoided errors, and the evaluations and raises that follow.
Over 10 years, the arithmetic is simple.
Nora earns 10 years × 1,700 decisions × $6,000 × 0.1% ≈ $102,000 more than a colleague of average ability in her position would earn.

The same trait, expressed equally in every decision and with the same effect per dollar at stake, is ten times as consequential for Nora as for Ben, and the entire difference lies in the situations the two encounter.

Four quantities did all the work: how many relevant situations the person encounters per year (1,700 or 1,500 decisions), over how many years (10), how strongly the trait shows in what the person does in each situation (here, equally in every decision), and what one instance of that behavior does to the outcome (here, 0.1% of the stakes, so that it depends on a feature of the situation).
Multiplying the four gives the trait's effect on the outcome for that person.
The PNT framework is the general statement of this arithmetic.
Because the four factors multiply and three of them depend on the situations the person encounters, two consequences follow.
First, the same trait can be powerful for one person and inert for another, so that population averages can conceal large effects.
Second, the narrow traits worth measuring for a given outcome can be found by starting from the situations that produce the outcome, rather than chosen by intuition.

A narrow trait, denoted n, is a specific individual-difference characteristic with high temporal stability.

Narrow personality traits are often referred to as personality nuances that are more specific than facets and much more specific than domains in standard personality inventories (Condon et al., 2020; Mõttus et al., 2017).

text.text: That said, "narrow trait" is not limited to personality nuances.
It also includes specific cognitive abilities and other temporally stable individual differences.

Examples of narrow traits include talkativeness as a nuance within the extraversion domain, reactive aggression as a nuance within the agreeableness domain, quantitative reasoning as a specific cognitive ability (often classified under fluid intelligence depending on the model), exercise adherence as a nuance within the conscientiousness domain, and rejection sensitivity as a nuance within the neuroticism domain.
These examples deliberately span a range of cultural generality, and PNT applies uniformly across this range.
Basic tendencies such as talkativeness, reactive aggression, and rejection sensitivity are expressed in situations that occur in most cultural contexts.
Characteristic adaptations such as quantitative reasoning and exercise adherence are expressed in situations that exist only where technology or institutions create them (e.g., McCrae & Costa, 2008).

text.text: Culture thus enters PNT through the situations it makes available and how often they occur (see Prediction 1), not as a situation feature itself.
A person p has a score on narrow trait n.
For convenience, I denote the person's standardized score as z(p), representing the number of standard deviations p deviates from the sample mean.
The index n is omitted because the equations treat one narrow trait at a time.
Where several traits enter jointly, the trait is indexed.

Each narrow trait n has an associated region X(n, Y) of the space of situation features in which n can be expressed as a state and that state has a non-negligible causal effect on the outcome Y. A situation is described by a vector of features, denoted x, that determine the affordances, demands, and constraints it presents (Gibson, 1977; Rauthmann et al., 2015).

A situation is described by a vector of features, denoted x, that determine the affordances, demands, and constraints it presents <ref type="bibr" target="#b44">(Gibson, 1977;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b98">Rauthmann et al., 2015)</ref>.

text.text: Features can be continuous or ordered (how many people are present, how much money is at stake, how strongly a setting discourages conversation) or present versus absent (whether a decision involves quantities at all).
The PNT framework does not commit to any particular taxonomy of situation features.
It does require that the features be scored on the situation itself rather than on how the focal person perceives it, and that they be as narrow as the trait, as explained below.

Researchers may draw on existing taxonomies such as DIAMONDS (Rauthmann et al., 2014) or CAPTION (Parrigon et al., 2017), domain-specific feature sets tailored to the trait of interest, or bottom-up feature sets derived empirically for the trait-outcome link at hand.

text.text: Which features matter, and over which range, depends on the narrow trait, the state through which it is expressed, and the outcomes under investigation.
For talkativeness, for example, the region X(n, Y) comprises the situations in which social interaction is possible and verbal behavior can unfold.

Within this region, narrower features such as the number of people present, how familiar they are, and how far the activity permits conversation plausibly shift both how strongly talkativeness translates into the state and how strongly that state causes the outcome of interest.

Breakfast with family members, commuting on public transit alongside strangers, and waiting with peers for a university lecture to start are points in this feature space: they differ in the familiarity of those present, their number, and the openness of the activity to conversation.
Which part of the space belongs to X(n, Y) depends on the outcome.
For subjective well-being, all three plausibly lie inside it.
For the number of new friendships formed, situations in which everyone present is already a close tie, such as breakfast with family members, contribute nothing, because no new tie can result.
The region is thus indexed by trait and outcome jointly.
This is also what keeps the problem tractable: parts of the feature space can often be excluded on theoretical grounds before any parameter is estimated.
Situation features are scored by criteria that do not depend on the focal person's construal, so that exposure tracks situation contact rather than situation perception.
Two kinds of criteria qualify.
The first are observable cues: who is present, where, and doing what (Johns, 2006; Rauthmann et al., 2015; Saucier et al., 2007), which can be counted and coded.

text.text: The second are psychological characteristics rated by observers or by consensus rather than by the focal person alone, for example how much a situation offers an opportunity to gain status (cf. Rauthmann et al., 2014).

text.text: The existing dimensional taxonomies were developed as measures of situation perception.
Used as features here, their dimensions must be scored by others or from coded cues, because self-scored features would confound exposure with construal.
Either way, the features must be as narrow as the trait.

A narrow trait is expressed in response to specific affordances, and a broad situation dimension averages over affordances that differ in whether they make the state possible and consequential, which blurs trait expressivity and the causal effect of the expressed state on the outcome in the same way that a broad trait blurs the effects of its components.
Narrowness is required on both sides.

For each person p, there is a long-run exposure density f(x | p): integrated over any range of feature values, it gives the expected number of objectively scorable instances per year that person p encounters with features in that range.
Integrating over all of X(n, Y) gives N(p), the number of relevant situations the person encounters per year, and f(x | p)/N(p) is the distribution of the person's situations over the features.

A representative sample of the person's situations, each scored on the features, estimates the distribution, and the number of instances per year scales it (see Measurement of Expressivity and Exposure).

A life outcome Y is, formally, a person-level variable, realized over a time horizon T, on which the expressed state has a well-defined causal effect and which is not itself an aggregate of that state.
Whether such a variable counts as a life outcome involves a further judgment about which end states matter.
That judgment is normative rather than formal (Wessels et al., 2016).

In a situation with features x, the state through which narrow trait n is expressed by person p is modeled as where α(x) is the average state level in situations with features x, β(n, x) is the trait expressivity at x (how strongly individual differences in the narrow trait are translated into differences in the expressed state in situations with those features), and ε captures residual variation from unmodeled factors.

In words, a person's state in a situation is the state an average person shows there, plus a deviation that grows with the person's trait level at a rate set by how much the situation lets the trait show, plus noise.
The term "state" encompasses behavior (e.g., speaking, exercising) as well as affect, cognitions, and desires (e.g., ruminating, experiencing pride, suppressing an impulse, wanting to impress).
Behavior is the paradigmatic case.

Where a trait is a capacity (e.g., quantitative reasoning) rather than a tendency (e.g., talkativeness), the state is the momentary performance in which the capacity is exercised (e.g., the quality of a quantitative decision, as in Box 1), and S is its level on the dimension that is causally relevant to Y.
Trait expressivity β(n, x) is trait-and situation-specific: it varies across the feature space, within and beyond X(n, Y).

It is zero in two cases: where the state cannot occur at all, because the situation does not afford it, and where the situation fixes the state at the same level for everyone, so that the state occurs but does not vary with the trait.
In the second case α can be substantial even though β is zero.

Note that situations outside X(n, Y) may nonetheless have substantial β, if the state is expressed there but has no consequence for Y. Situational strength is itself a feature, or a combination of features, along which β is expected to decline: classical and recent accounts suggest that β is smaller in strong situations than in weak situations, because strong situations constrain decision-making freedom and limit the range of individually differentiated behavior (Judge & Zapata, 2015; Meyer et al., 2010; Mischel, 1977).

text.text: The framework is agnostic on the precise form of β and treats it as an empirically estimated function.

Estimating it requires pooling instances with similar features, either by assuming a functional form (β linear in a feature, say, estimated as a trait × feature interaction) or by smoothing across neighboring feature values.
How much β varies across the feature space is itself an empirical question.
In everyday experience-sampling data, situational differences in trait-state slopes have been modest relative to individual differences in situation-state contingencies (Kuper et al., 2024).

text.text: I compare two employees, Nora and Ben, matched on trait level (both z = +1) but working in different occupational niches.
The relevant situations are quantitative decisions at work, and the situation feature x is the amount at stake in a decision, in dollars, which is scored from the decision itself.
Quantifying the four factors.
Exposure as a distribution over the feature f(x | p).
Both make a similar number of quantitative decisions per year, but the stakes differ.

Nora, a portfolio analyst, makes about N ≈ 1,700 decisions per year with stakes that are lognormally distributed with a median of about $1,900 and a mean of m ≈ $6,000, so she handles roughly $10.2 million of stakes per year.
Ben, a communications manager, makes about N ≈ 1,500 decisions per year with a median of about $230 and a mean of m ≈ $700, roughly $1.05 million per year.
Time horizon T. 10 years for both.
A 1-SD advantage yields the same increment in decision quality whatever the stakes: β ≈ 1.0 quality units per decision per SD, constant in x.

The earnings consequence of a quality unit grows with the stakes: γ(x) ≈ κ × x with κ = 0.001, that is, one quality unit changes cumulative income by 0.1% of the amount at stake: $0.05 for a $50 task and $50 for a $50,000 valuation, where a sound valuation or an avoided costly error feeds into evaluations, advancement, and compensation.
Putting the four factors together.
Applying Equation 3: with β constant and γ = κ × x, the average of β × γ over a person's decisions is β × κ × m, so ΔY = T × β × κ × N × m × z.

For Nora, this is roughly a 10% gain in annual earnings per SD, which is conservative relative to the ≈18% average per-SD return to numeracy among prime-age workers in OECD countries (Hanushek et al., 2015).

text.text: Exposure is estimated without classifying any decision: a sample of each person's decisions with their stakes recorded gives m, and the number of decisions per year gives N. and Quantitative Reasoning Figure 1 plots ΔY (in U.S. dollars) as a function of the total stakes of quantitative decisions handled per year, N × m, the only quantity on which Ben and Nora differ.
Because γ is linear in the stakes, ΔY is a straight line through the origin for each trait level; at z = 1, it is 0.1% of each year's stakes, accumulated over 10 years.
What this illustrates.
Despite identical trait levels, Nora's trait-attributable income exceeds Ben's tenfold, driven entirely by the stakes of the decisions she encounters.
The contrast is carried by γ, not β: the ability is expressed about equally in small and large decisions, but only the latter carry appreciable earnings stakes.
For illustration, β is constant and γ linear in the stakes, the state is linear in trait level, and effects are additive across situations.
Calibration details and the assumptions relaxed in the Extensions are given in the online supplement (Text S1).
In Equation 1, β(n, x) is not person-specific: it describes the average slope with which individual differences in n translate into the state in situations with features x.
The framework can accommodate person-specific expressivity by allowing person-specific slopes β(n, x, p) = β(n, x) + η(n, x, p), where η captures person p's deviation from the population slope.

Like the other person-specific parameters in Table 1, η is defined counterfactually, as the amount by which person p's state in situations with features x would change per SD of the trait, over and above the population slope.

text.text: For readability, the equations below use the population slope β(n, x); substituting β(n, x, p) yields the fully person-specific form.

Equations 2 and 3 below use only the slope β but not the average state level α, because α is trait-independent: under their assumptions it is shared by a person and their mean-level (z = 0) counterfactual and cancels from the trait-attributable deviation.
It re-enters once exposure itself depends on the trait, as in the selection extension, or once the outcome depends nonlinearly on cumulated state, as under the diminishing returns extension.
I return to both extensions below.

In a situation with features x, the expressed state S(n, x, p) produces an effect on the outcome Y. Let γ(x, Y | p) denote the person-specific average causal effect of a unit increase in S on Y in one instance of a situation with features x.
The effect need not materialize within the situation.

It includes consequences that unfold later, through mediators (exercising affects mortality through fitness; see Life Outcome), through others' memories and reactions (Back et al., 2011), and through the person's own later reflection on the episode.

text.text: The qualifier withinsituation therefore refers to where the state is expressed, not to when its consequences occur.
In some settings γ will be homogeneous across persons.
In many settings γ varies across persons for biological, contextual, or structural reasons (e.g., Bryan et al., 2021; Denissen et al., 2018; Wenzel et al., 2025).

text.text: Because γ is the effect of a single instance of the expressed state, it is typically very small in absolute terms (see Box 1) and cannot be read off any one instance.

Estimating it requires aggregating the state-outcome relationship across many instances or many persons, as discussed below under Estimating the Within-Situation Causal Efficacy, and, like β, pooling instances with similar features.
The talkativeness example introduced earlier shows why β and γ must be carried as separate functions of the features.

Talkativeness is expressed most fully among familiar others, as at breakfast with family members, less fully among waiting peers, and least among commuting strangers, where norms discourage unsolicited conversation: β declines as the people present become less familiar.
The per-instance effect on forming a new friendship plausibly runs in the opposite direction: γ rises as they become less familiar, because only a new tie can become a new friendship.
Box 1 presents a complementary case, in which β is roughly constant across the feature space and the entire contrast is carried by γ.

Assuming additive cumulation of within-situation effects over the time horizon T (in years) across which outcome Y is defined, the expected contribution of person p's standardized score z on narrow trait n to outcome Y is

In words, the trait's contribution to the outcome is the person's trait level times a coefficient, the Power of the Narrow Trait n for outcome Y in person p: the difference between the person's expected outcome and the outcome the same person would have at the mean trait level, per SD of z (derivation in Text S2).

This coefficient multiplies the four factors at each point of the feature space and sums over the situations the person encounters: where N(p) is the number of relevant situations person p encounters per year, Ex | p[•] is the average over those situations, that is, over the person's distribution of situations across the features, and the integral in the second line runs over the region X(n, Y), with f(x | p) equal to N(p) times that distribution.

In words, the power of a narrow trait is years × relevant situations per year × the average, over the situations the person encounters, of how strongly the trait shows in the state times what one unit of the state does to the outcome.
The first line of Equation 3 is how the coefficient is estimated in practice: β × γ is averaged over a representative sample of the person's situations and multiplied by N(p) and T.
The second line writes the same quantity as an integral over the feature space, the form on which the extensions below build.

Where β × γ is approximately linear in the features, only the means of the features over the person's situations matter, as in Box 1; where it is not, the shape of the exposure distribution matters as well.

Because the factors multiply, even a trait that is strongly expressed (high β) and highly consequential per instance (high γ) has negligible power when the situations that afford it are rare (low N(p)).
Thus, the same trait can be powerful for one person, population, or outcome and inert for another (see Box 1).

The same arithmetic explains the appeal of broad traits: a domain pools narrow traits that are expressed across many regions of the feature space, so its summed exposure is large even when no single component is powerful.
The population-average PNT is obtained by taking expectations over persons:
In words, the population-average power of a narrow trait is the average of its person-specific power over the persons in the population.

text.text: A near-zero population-average PNT is therefore ambiguous between three very different realities: (a) a trait that matters little for anyone; (b) one that matters substantially but only for a small, same-direction subgroup (dilution); or (c) one that matters greatly in opposing directions across the niches the average pools over (cancellation).
Distinguishing them requires disaggregating by situational niche.

The basic PNT equations (Equations 2 and 3) assume additive cumulation of withinsituation effects, linear expression of narrow traits in the state, and situation exposure f given exogenously as an input.
None of these assumptions is strictly necessary.
Four extensions are worth noting briefly.

These extensions complicate the equations but not the substantive claims: relaxing additivity or exogenous exposure alters the magnitude and shape of trait-outcome effects, not the four factors that govern them.
Outcomes might depend on the cumulation of states with diminishing returns.

For example, the effect of an exercise adherence nuance on all-cause mortality is governed by a saturating relationship between cumulative weekly physical activity and mortality risk reduction (Han et al., 2026; Stamatakis et al., 2025).

text.text: I apply it to two otherwise identical 50-year-old women who enter at different trait levels: Judith moves from z = -1 to 0, Lara from z = +1 to +2.
The outcome is 20-year all-cause mortality probability.
Quantifying the four factors.
Exposure f(x | p).

The relevant situations are planned exercise opportunities, described by one feature, x: how costly fatigue or competing demands make initiation at that opportunity, from 0 (no cost) to 1 (high cost).
Both women encounter about 5 opportunities per week, N ≈ 260 per year, spread roughly evenly over the range of x.
Time horizon T. 20 years.

The nuance makes a difference only where initiation is costly: one SD more adds no moderate-to-vigorous physical activity (MVPA) at an opportunity that costs nothing to start (x = 0) and about 12 minutes at the costliest opportunities (x = 1), that is, β(n, x) ≈ 12 × x minutes per opportunity per SD.
Averaged over the opportunities encountered, which are spread evenly over x, so that the mean x is 0.5, this is 6 minutes per opportunity, or 30 min/week.
With the mean-level person at 30 min/week of MVPA from these opportunities, Judith moves from 0 to 30 min/week and Lara from 60 to 90, the same +30 min/week increment.

Because MVPAmortality associations saturate with weekly dose (Han et al., 2026; Stamatakis et al., 2025), I replace the linear γ with the marginal slope of a saturating function of weekly MVPA D, g(D) = 0.25 × [1 -exp(-D / 75)], calibrated so that moving from 0 to ≈ 150 min/week yields a ≈ 22% relative hazard reduction (Koemel et al., 2026; Stamatakis et al., 2025).

text.text: The 20-year mortality probability at D = 0 is ≈ 0.15.
Putting the factors together.
N, the distribution of x, β(n, x), T, and the +1 SD increment are identical for both women; only γ-the slope of g at each woman's current MVPA level-differs.

Judith's 20-year mortality probability falls from 0.150 to 0.138 (-1.2 percentage points), Lara's from 0.129 to 0.124 (-0.6 points): the same intervention yields about twice the benefit for Judith, because she begins in the steep region of the dose-response curve.

Figure 2 traces both trajectories along the dose-response curve: the arrows have identical horizontal length (+30 min/week), but Judith's traverses the steep region while Lara's lies in the flattening shoulder, and the projected mortality reductions (vertical bars) differ twofold.

The trait maps linearly onto behavior (+30 min/week per SD), but behavior maps onto the outcome through the saturating g, so γ is not a fixed coefficient but the slope of g at the behavior a person already produces, which itself depends on z.
Values are illustrative order-of-magnitude calibrations, not parameter estimates, and g(•) is stylized; calibration details are in the online supplement (Text S1).

The baseline form cumulates within-situation effects additively across the time window T, which fits monotonically nondecreasing outcomes most directly. Wessels et al.'s (2016) remaining trajectory classes call for different aggregation operators over time: single-switch binary outcomes such as mortality for a hazard-rate form, reversible binary outcomes such as marital status for a state-transition form, and freely varying outcomes such as well-being for a time-weighted kernel that down-weights more distant behavior (the device already introduced in Footnote 1 for recency-dependent outcomes).

text.text: In each case the four ingredients (f, T, β, γ) remain the only quantities required, and only the rule by which within-situation effects are summed over time changes.
These reformulations are compatible with the decomposition but each adds estimation burden.
The basic equation is additive in two respects.
First, it integrates within-situation effects across the situations in which a trait is expressed.
Second, when several narrow traits bear on an outcome, it implicitly sums their separate contributions.
For some outcomes neither additivity holds, because the effect of a behavior depends on what else the person does, whether in another situation or as the expression of another trait.

Across situations, joint analyses of sleep, physical activity, and nutrition suggest that the three behaviors interact synergistically in their association with all-cause mortality, with combinations producing risk reductions that exceed what any single behavior achieves in isolation (Stamatakis et al., 2025; see also Han et al., 2026).

text.text: Across traits, behavioral tendencies can compensate for or facilitate one another: a high level on one narrow trait can substitute for a low level on another (sub-additive), or two tendencies can be jointly more consequential than their separate effects would imply (super-additive).
For instance, conscientiousness and interest seem to partly compensate in producing academic effort and achievement (e.g., Bareis et al., 2024; Trautwein et al., 2015).
text.formatted: For instance, conscientiousness and interest seem to partly compensate in producing academic effort and achievement (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">Bareis et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b116">Trautwein et al., 2015)</ref>.

text.text: In both cases the contribution of one behavior is conditional on another, and both are absorbed by letting γ(x, Y | p) depend on the joint behavioral configuration rather than on a single behavior in isolation.
When the interacting behaviors occur in situations with different features, γ generalizes to γ(x, x′, Y | p).
When they are driven by different narrow traits, γ generalizes to an analogous cross-trait term.
The corresponding aggregation then turns from additive to bilinear.
The basic equation takes situation exposure f as an exogenous input.

In reality, however, exposure is itself partly a consequence of narrow traits, because individuals actively shape the distribution of situations they encounter (e.g., Kuper, Breitmoser, et al., 2025; Rauthmann et al., 2015; Trappes et al., 2022; Wagerman & Funder, 2009; Xi & Jackson, 2026).

Trappes et al. (2022) define three mechanisms by which individuals shape their fit with their environments (niche choice, niche conformance, and niche construction), and Kuper, Breitmoser, and colleagues (2025) map these mechanisms across disciplines.

(2022)</ref> define three mechanisms by which individuals shape their fit with their environments (niche choice, niche conformance, and niche construction), and Kuper, Breitmoser, and colleagues (2025) map these mechanisms across disciplines.

text.text: Two of them bear on exposure.
Niche choice refers to the individual selecting into environments that fit their tendencies (e.g., a more talkative student joining more student clubs).
Niche construction refers to the individual changing the properties of environments they already inhabit (e.g., a more talkative student turning a quiet study group into a lively one).
Choice changes which situations the person enters.
It typically raises f in trait-congruent regions of the feature space and lowers it elsewhere.
Trait-congruent regions are those in which the trait is readily expressed (higher β) or its expression pays (higher γ).

Construction changes the features of the situations the person already occupies, which moves them to another point of the feature space (the study group made lively moves from the quiet to the lively part), so construction also shifts f, typically toward traitcongruent regions.

A dynamic extension of PNT accommodates both mechanisms by treating the situation exposure density f as a function of the narrow-trait level z rather than as a fixed input: where f₀(x | p) is the person's baseline exposure density that would obtain in the absence of trait-driven choice and construction, and λ(x) is a composite trait-to-exposure slope that aggregates over both.

In words, each SD of the trait adds λ(x) situations per year at feature configuration x, or removes them where λ is negative, and exposure cannot fall below zero. λ is positive where situation selection is trait-congruent (e.g., talkative people selecting situations in which they can talk), but can also be negative where it is trait-incongruent.
For example, people high in self-control avoid tempting situations (Ent et al., 2015; see Text S4 and Figure S1).
text.formatted: For example, people high in self-control avoid tempting situations <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">(Ent et al., 2015</ref>; see Text S4 and Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">S1</ref>).

If so, trait self-control pays off less through resisting temptation (β) than through avoiding or removing it (λ).

In words, the trait's contribution is now the sum, over the situations the person actually encounters, of what each instance of the state does to the outcome, minus the same sum for a person of average trait level, who encounters different situations.

Once α no longer cancels, the zero point of the state matters: S = 0 must be the level at which an instance contributes nothing to Y. For most states this is the natural zero (saying nothing in a conversation yields no social capital), but not for all: exerting no self-control in a tempting situation means yielding, which harms Y. Such a state is scaled to the no-contribution zero instead, so that the person who yields has a negative S, and Equations 8 and 9 then hold as written (Text S4, Figure S1).

text.text: In this case, the selection-and-construction channel carries the sign of z.
High-z persons gain exposure to situations that pay, and low-z persons forgo it, so selection amplifies on both sides.
On the high side, the quadratic part of this channel (λβγz²) adds to its linear part (λαγz), so advantages accelerate super-linearly.
On the low side, the quadratic part offsets the linear part, so disadvantages deepen without accelerating.
Because exposure cannot fall below zero, the low side is bounded by full withdrawal, whereas the high side is unbounded.

The avoidance case, trait-incongruent selection (λ < 0) away from situations in which the state harms Y (α + βz ≤ 0), is the mirror image: high-z persons shed harmful exposure and low-z persons accumulate it, so disadvantages accelerate on the low side and the withdrawal bound lies on the high side (Text S4, Figure S1).

As a template, the PNT framework is not refuted by any single observation, because it is close to definitional that a trait's effect is carried by its manifestations in situations.

In addition, departures from the basic form, such as non-additive aggregation, diminishing returns, and traitdependent exposure, are absorbed by the proposed extensions or, where none fits, by new ones Prediction 1: Exposure-dependent group differences.

The causal effect of n on Y differs across groups (occupations, sexes, cultures) that meet the outcome-relevant situations at different rates, in proportion to T × ∫ₓ (f × β × γ) dx within each group.
Even where β and γ are comparable, PNT differs when the outcome-relevant situations are rare in one group and frequent in another.

text.text: Prediction 2: PNT weights are person-and group-specific.
How much a trait counts depends on the person's situation exposure: a trait's weight in a composite of narrow traits that predicts Y is its PNT coefficient.
Thus, composites with person-specific PNT weights out-predict fixed-weight composites of the same traits in samples with heterogeneous exposure.

Groups differ as well: people who differ in parenthood, occupation, health, relationship status, or cultural context can differ systematically in f, β, and γ (e.g., for occupations, Denissen et al., 2018; for β across countries, Kuper et al., 2026; on the group-specificity of principles more generally, Kuper, Breitmoser, et al., 2025).

text.text: Because the three factors multiply, their group differences can reinforce or offset one another, so that a narrow trait with large PNT for one group can have near-zero PNT for another, and weights estimated in one group transfer to another only after re-weighting by the target group's f (and, where β and γ differ as well, re-estimating them).

The alternative is a purely statistical account that estimates item-or nuance-level weights by penalized regression, with no structural interpretation and no mechanism for re-weighting across persons or groups.

The discriminating implication is that PNT names what must be re-estimated (at a minimum f) and predicts a gain from person-specific weighting and from f-re-weighting that grows with the heterogeneity of f.

The test is an out-of-sample comparison of person-specific PNT weights, fixed weights, and broad-trait scores in heterogeneous samples, and a cross-group validation of transferred versus f-re-weighted weights.

text.text: The PNT framework implies that trait-outcome studies should assess not only the trait and the outcome but also the frequency of relevant situations, trait expressivity, and the effect of the expressed state on the outcome to clarify when and why a trait leads to an outcome.
Concretely, the framework proposes a three-step measurement pipeline.
First, specify the outcome Y, the target population, and the relevant time window T. Second, enumerate potentially relevant candidate narrow traits and their associated situation regions X(n, Y).

This can be done using taxonomic and behavioral resources such as trait taxonomies (e.g., Ashton et al., 2004; Bainbridge et al., 2022; Henry & Mõttus, 2025), situation taxonomies (Parrigon et al., 2017; Rauthmann et al., 2014), and occupational task databases (e.g., O*NET, 2024).

text.text: Third, for each candidate narrow trait, measure and estimate the PNT components: population-average situation exposure (e.g., from diary or census data), trait expressivity (e.g., from experience sampling), and within-situation efficacy (e.g., from longitudinal, quasi-experimental, or ideally experimental designs).
Because assessment over the full horizon T is rarely feasible, the parameters can be measured in a random sample of time intervals and extrapolated over T (Wessels et al., 2016).

text.text: Candidate traits are then ranked by their expected PNT, and components whose variation does not materially change the implied effect can be fixed at default values, concentrating measurement effort where it matters.
Implementing this third step in practice involves measuring both trait expression and situation frequency at the level of specific situation features.
Narrow-trait inventories typically present items detached from situational anchors ("I am talkative").

One way to assess trait expressivity might be to explicitly situate items (cf. the frame-of-reference tradition; Holtrop et al., 2014), with each item identifying a recurring configuration of situation features and asking about typical behavior in situations of that kind ("In informal conversations with friends or family, I tend to speak frequently and at length").

text.text: To capture not only expression but also exposure, each expressivity item should be paired with a brief situation-frequency item ("How often do you have informal conversations with friends or family in a typical week?").

The expressivity item provides an estimate of β, the frequency item provides an estimate of f, and together they yield the f × β contribution of situations with those features to person-specific PNT at the item-pair level.

Estimating γ poses a distinctive challenge.

By construction, γ is the effect of a single instance of the expressed state, which is typically a small fraction of an outcome event or of a standard deviation of the outcome (Boxes 1-3) and too small to reliably detect in any single instance.

It becomes estimable only after the within-situation state-outcome relationship has been aggregated, across the many instances of situations with similar features that one person encounters over time or across many persons who differ in how much trait-relevant state expression they produce.

The target of estimation is the average per-instance slope of the outcome on the state, which, multiplied by expressivity and scaled by exposure and time, reproduces the causal effect of n on Y (Equation 3).

text.text: Confounding is the central obstacle to estimating γ.

The quantity of the state a person expresses in situations with given features is not randomly assigned: it covaries with other states, with stable dispositions, and with features of the situations the person occupies, each of which can affect Y through paths that bypass the focal state.
Regressing the outcome on the aggregated state therefore conflates γ with the effects of these correlated causes.

The cleanest estimates of γ accordingly come from designs that sever this dependence: experimental manipulation of the state in situations with given features (e.g., Schmiedek & Neubauer, 2020), or natural and quasiexperiments that supply exogenous variation in the state or at least in situational exposure (Grosz, Ayaita, et al., 2024).

The PNT framework combines these traditions and formalizes a step they describe only verbally: the rule by which within-episode consequences aggregate over situations and time into long-run outcomes.
The PNT framework is bounded by several assumptions and leaves several questions open.
First, it assumes that the situations in which the state is expressed can be meaningfully described by features.
For many states this is straightforward.

For diffuse affective states or generalized mood it is not, and extending PNT to non-situational domains will require further work, perhaps through integration with distinct-emotions research (Mercadante et al., 2025).

text.text: A related open problem is how finely β and γ should be allowed to vary with the features.
A functional form that is too rigid hides variation that matters, whereas one that is too flexible cannot be estimated from the situations a person encounters.

Second, narrow-trait levels are treated as stable over T. For outcomes that cumulate over decades, within-person change can be substantial (Bleidorn et al., 2022), including change that feeds back from a person's own states through reflection (Wrzus & Roberts, 2017).

Experiments remedy confounding but face two further difficulties.
First, manipulating one behavior typically perturbs other behaviors, attention, and contextual cues (fat-handedness; Eronen, 2020).
Second, self-reported outcomes are susceptible to demand effects (Corneille & Lush, 2023).

text.text: The PNT framework does not dissolve these problems, but it localizes them to within-situation state-outcome links of narrow traits, which are more amenable to manipulation than trait-outcome links of broad traits.
Its γ tests are likely most informative for extrapsychological outcomes (income, academic achievement, social status, objectively measured health).

Finally, the framework is silent on the origins of individual differences in its components (why persons differ in f, β, or γ), which require theories about genetic and environmental influences, development, socialization, and selection.

Of the features, sources, and outcomes of individuality distinguished by Kuper, Breitmoser, et al. (2025), PNT addresses the outcomes and takes the rest as given, which is also a programmatic commitment to start from outcomes rather than traits.

The PNT framework thereby turns a set of longrecognized but loosely connected intuitions into a structure that is precise enough to explain trait-outcome links once its components are estimated, to test in its calibrated instances, and to intervene on.

An instance of the framework, in contrast, is refutable.
In an instance, a trait, outcome, population, situation region X(n, Y), and aggregation rule are specified in advance, and f, β, and γ are estimated independently.

One can therefore test whether the effect composed from the components of an instance reproduces the trait's causally identified effect, which is what van Dongen et al. (2025) require of a theory that explains a phenomenon.
Beyond this, the framework makes at least six predictions on which rival accounts predict otherwise.
These predictions, too, are stated for instances.

text.text: Their model gives four reasons why life outcomes are hard to predict: P and E are dynamic and plural, they interact, error is substantial, and low base rates and range restriction attenuate observed associations.
PNT accepts these reasons but specifies, for a given narrow trait, the part of that function that runs through behavior.

The four factors in Equation 3 (situation exposure frequency, time horizon, trait expressivity, and within-situation causal efficacy) are a formal account of where a narrow trait's effect on an outcome comes from, complementary to Liou et al.'s account of why observed prediction is bounded.

Because PNT prescribes measures that conventional prediction studies omit, it treats part of that bound as a measurement gap rather than as inherent (Prediction 5; Text situations and time into life outcomes, with every term of that rule explicit and estimable.
It specifies exactly what information is lost when researchers work at the trait-outcome level and exactly what additional measurement is required.
Two lessons stand out: First, the field has long measured traits and outcomes but has left unmeasured the rate at which outcome-relevant situations occur.
Yet this rate is often decisive and varies sharply across persons and groups.
